title: Macau jails pro-democracy campaigner in city's first national security case
description: Macau has sentenced an ex-lawmaker and pro-democracy campaigner to 12 years and six months' jail in the city's first national security case.Following
body: Macau has sentenced an ex-lawmaker and pro-democracy campaigner to 12 years and six months' jail in the city's first national security case.Following a closed-door trial, Au Kam San, 69, was convicted on Friday of "subversion against the political power of the state", among other offences.His wife Virginia Cheang condemned the ruling, calling the case a "groundless persecution designed to humiliate Au".Macau was handed back to China in 1999, ending over 400 years of Portuguese administration. Its national security law came into effect in 2009, criminalising acts of treason, secession, and subversion against the Chinese Communist Party.The law was revised in 2023, broadening its scope to include non-violent acts of secession, and again this year, to allow for trials to be held behind closed doors.Prosecutors had accused Au of assisting and collaborating with "external hostile organisations" by collecting, preparing and disseminating information that was "manifestly filled with political claims of a subversive nature against the state".These took place "over a long period of time", the prosecutors claim.Au was arrested in July 2025 and later charged with three counts of subverting the state's power, three counts of endangering national security by establishing contact with foreign organisations, and one count of breach of confidentiality.He was found guilty of four of the seven charges following a three-day trial which ended in September. A judge had ordered that the trial be held behind closed doors "to ensure that no prejudice is caused to the interests of national security".Macau's authorities never publicly disclosed the details of the case. Au's family had earlier told the media Au was not allowed to seek his own legal representation and had instead been assigned a lawyer by the court.Au's wife Cheang said she hoped authorities would grant her and her family permission to regularly write to and visit Au in prison."I dare not hope for more as I believe that will only lead to greater disappointment," she said in an open letter on Friday.Au, who was formerly a primary school teacher, was elected to the Legislative Assembly in September 2001. For 20 years, he served as one of only a handful of pro-democracy lawmakers in the legislature, largely made up of pro-Beijing loyalists.Au had co-organised annual vigils in Macau to commemorate the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown in Beijing. These vigils were previously tolerated in places like Macau and Hong Kong, but have effectively been banned in both cities since China imposed a sweeping national security law on Hong Kong in 2020.Au's jailing comes a day after Hong Kong sentenced Joshua Wong, the face of its now-quashed democracy movement, to 10 years in jail. Wong, 30, whose activism started when he was just a teen, has been in custody for the last six years.

schema.headline: Macau jails pro-democracy campaigner in city's first national security case

title: Paraguay President Santiago Peña resigns after bank collapse
description: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña has announced his resignation following a political crisis sparked by the collapse of a bank linked to him."I want
body: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña has announced his resignation following a political crisis sparked by the collapse of a bank linked to him."I want to apologise to the people if at any point I failed," he said in a video message on social media. "It was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me." The crisis erupted after Ueno Bank entered an insolvency process, which froze all operations. Lawmakers accused Peña, who was a shareholder until last year in the company that owned the bank, of conflicts of interest and misconduct.Peña rejected suggestions of impropriety. His resignation came as Paraguay's lower house of congress voted in favour of pursuing an impeachment trial.Photos taken near Paraguay's Congress building on Thursday show police officers clashing with protesters demanding Peña be removed from office.Paraguay's congress must approve the resignation of a president. But a special session convened on Thursday to address his resignation was adjourned in favour of continuing with the impeachment process.Congress has scheduled a special session for Friday, when Peña is expected to present his defence, according to Reuters news agency. In a post on X, Peña confirmed he would appear for Senate impeachment proceedings, adding that he would do so to "exercise my right to a defence".He wrote: "I will provide the information requested of me. Citizens deserve to know the truth, without cover-ups and without anyone being above the law."Peña earlier said his resignation was to protect stability, social peace and democratic institutions.Ueno Bank has said it has about three million customers, equivalent to about 60% of Paraguay's adult population.It held pensions and some other public funds and, after its collapse earlier this week, millions could not access their accounts. The central bank seized the digital lender, and people took to the streets protesting and demanding Peña's resignation.A new president of the Central Bank of Paraguay has been appointed and Congress has approved a process to pay depositors.

schema.headline: Paraguay President Santiago Peña resigns after bank collapse

title: AI stocks bounce back after trillions wiped from market values
description: Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms have recovered slightly from an enormous sell-off that wiped trillions of dollars off stock val
body: Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms have recovered slightly from an enormous sell-off that wiped trillions of dollars off stock values.The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index closed in positive territory following a market rout that began in the US on Thursday before spilling over to Asian and European markets into Friday.Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat victory in the midterm elections would mean slower artificial intelligence development.However the latest US employment figures added to a mixed picture for American markets on Friday morning, with an unexpectedly strong 165,000 jobs added to the economy in September.On Thursday, businesses closely linked to artificial intelligence development took a hammering on stock markets, particularly chip and semiconductor makers.But the Nasdaq Composite bounced back slightly on Friday, ending the day up 1.1%, partly reversing some of its 5.5% fall. The S&P 500, which tracks the share prices of the largest publicly-traded US companies, closed up 0.3%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was flat through the day before ending slightly down 0.4%.Companies that lost hundreds of billions in market value recovered some ground on Friday, including Nvidia, SpaceX and Tesla.However, stock markets in Asia and Europe fared worse.The Kospi in South Korea closed down 6% on Friday, with shares in chipmaker SK Hynix plunging more than 10%. European markets also fell, with the main indexes in Germany, France and Spain ending the day down.In the UK, the FTSE 100, which tracks the largest companies on the London Stock Exchange, declined 1.01%.In addition to the recent market volatility, UK traders were also digesting the latest Bank of England decision to raise interest rates and the signal that another rate rise could be on the cards to curb rising prices.The market fluctuations also come after the sweeping Democrat victory in the midterm elections.A number of Democrats campaigned for new rules and regulations for artificial intelligence (AI) and data centres, and the party has since won control of both houses of congress as well as key contests in states that have been part of the AI data centre race.US President Donald Trump on Friday reiterated his supported for what he calls "super intelligence", saying only "foolish leadership" would "say no to the riches they bring".However, there have also been concerns over whether the enormous amounts of money being spent on AI will pay off.Russ Shaw, founder of global tech advocacy firm Tech London Advocates, said the election result was sending a message that a rethink was needed on AI."The incoming Congress is going to really focus on AI in a very dramatic way," he told the BBC's Business Today."I'm a big fan of AI, but I'm watching what these companies are doing, and they're not communicating effectively at all, particularly in the US, about what the benefits of AI are all about."Pierre Baqué, chief executive of AI platform Neural Concept, said the share movements were a "necessary market correction" that reflected a legitimate concern about the amount of money being poured into AI infrastructure."The industry must move beyond unchecked infrastructure investment and demonstrate greater financial discipline," he said. "We are entering a critical transition phase, a market purgatory where raw tech must prove its widespread economic value."Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said it had been a brutal week for markets, and the key question was whether the jump in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq would be sustained."Once investors have had the weekend to catch their breath, next week could give a clearer indication of whether the tech trade is going down the pan or fighting back."

schema.headline: AI stocks bounce back after trillions wiped from market values

title: Will Nigeria's Atiku Abubakar be on the presidential ballot after ADC court ruling?
description: Several high-profile politicians joined the ADC in 2025 - disillusioned by the factional infighting in the once powerful Peoples Democratic Party (PDP
body: Several high-profile politicians joined the ADC in 2025 - disillusioned by the factional infighting in the once powerful Peoples Democratic Party (PDP).Among them were Abubakar - who had served as vice-president between 1999 and 2007 when the PDP was in power - and former Senate president David Mark.As accommodations were made for the line-up of political heavyweights, Mark took over as its interim chairman.But Nafiu Bala Gombe, a former ADC national deputy chairman, argued before the court that this was not lawful as Mark and others had not been elected at a national convention.Instead, he said, he himself should have taken over the party's leadership following the resignation of the ADC's former chairman in 2025.This is not first time the Federal High Court in the capital, Abuja, has ruled on the leadership of the party.In July, judge Musa Liman said Mark had been chosen in accordance with the country's laws and the party's constitution - in a case brought by another former ADC member.Abubakar said the latest case raised serious legal concerns: "Why, after that judgment, was another case filed to reopen the same dispute?"In a statement, the ADC added that Thursday's judgement by Justice Peter Lifu was aimed at stifling the opposition momentum and "was a calculated attempt to weaken the ADC and frustrate" Abubakar's candidacy.The ADC is seen as the most powerful opposition to President Tinubu. Many influential politicians opposed to the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) have already defected to the party.The legal saga could complicate things - it may cause uncertainty for hundreds of ADC candidates as well as raise questions over who has the authority to represent them.Peter Obi - the other main presidential candidate, who is on the ballot for a second time - said he was shocked by Thursday's high court ruling.He released a statement on X with the heading, external: "Do not undermine democracy".The 65-year-old went on to say: "My concern is that three months before a general election, it is in the public interest to have certainty.Obi had briefly joined the ADC before leaving earlier this year to join the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) - in part because of the legal challenges within the ADC."The sustenance of democracy in Nigeria, in the midst of encroaching military rule in West Africa, should strengthen our resolve to protect opposition politics and not stamp out opposition parties," he said.The NDC's candidate said that, as president, he would ensure that the existence of opposition parties would be respected. "This is a time to strengthen our democracy by allowing the opposition to thrive."Additional reporting by Chris Ewokor in Abuja

schema.headline: Will Nigeria's Atiku Abubakar be on the presidential ballot after ADC court ruling?

title: Major construction near Iran bases, satellite images suggest
description: ByShayan SardarizadehBenedict Garman and Matt MurphyBBC Verify  Iran appears to be undertaking significant new construction near at least two of its m
body: ByShayan SardarizadehBenedict Garman and Matt MurphyBBC Verify  Iran appears to be undertaking significant new construction near at least two of its major missile sites and repairing bases damaged by months of US and Israeli air strikes, analysis of satellite images suggests.Evidence of digging and new buildings are visible in satellite imagery taken in November at the Garmdareh military base in Karaj near the capital Tehran and the Shahroud base in the north, analysts at British intelligence company MAIAR, who reviewed the photos, told BBC Verify.At least 12 other military sites, including missile complexes and air bases, appear to show signs of repairs. New roofs have been built on destroyed buildings at the Kermanshah missile base in western Iran, near the border with Iraq, while damaged buildings and debris have been cleared at the Parchin military complex - which has been repeatedly repaired despite a succession of air strikes - east of the capital.The excavations near Shahroud could potentially be related to the production of missiles, said Jim Lamson, a former CIA analyst who focused on Iran. He said that because the nearby air base at Shahroud has been targeted multiple times in recent years, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) is probably trying to find ways to move its production facilities underground.A MAIAR analyst said that Iran has "a pattern of moving infrastructure underground to protect them from further strikes". Mark Mellett, a defence analyst and former head of the Irish military, said the construction of underground facilities had the added benefit of making it "harder for outside observers to assess the extent and operational status".Speculation has mounted in recent weeks that the US could resume attacks on Iran after the midterm elections held earlier this week. But on Wednesday Vice-President JD Vance cited the war's unpopularity with voters for the Republicans' poor performance in this week's poll, saying that it may have cost his party control of the Senate "for the next 6 years".At multiple bases across the country, Iranian forces have focused on carrying-out small-scale repairs to complexes which have been heavily damaged by air strikes since the start of the US-Israeli war. Analysts said that satellite images appear to show that significant construction has been completed at the Taleghan 2 facility at the Parchin military complex, with damaged buildings levelled and the aftermath of attacks on an underground bunker repaired and reinforced with concrete.At Karaj, external and Shahroud, satellite images appear to show significant excavation. At Karaj, multiple vehicles were visible in satellite images, while improvements appear to have been carried out to the nearby airbase.The images from Karaj appear to show "a new portal for an underground facility", said Sam Lair, research analyst at the Foreign Policy Research Institute (FPRI), which has looked extensively into recent developments at Iranian sites. Analysis from Janes also indicates there appears to be a new facility under construction at Karaj, including tunnel entrances and structures which could indicate an expansion of nearby damaged or destroyed missile bases - or could also be for storage or other purposes.The construction work is unlikely to be part of an effort to deceive foreign intelligence agencies, said Janes analyst Sean O'Connor. He said such a project "would be costly and may achieve little".The developments come after repeated assurances from the White House that US-Israeli attacks have depleted the Iranian armed forces, which US President Donald Trump dismissed as a "complete and total mess".A Pentagon spokesperson previously said that the US had "destroyed up to 90% of Iran's drone, ballistic missile, and naval industrial base" and "significantly degraded" the country's ability to launch drone and missile attacks.But Iran claims it retains large stockpiles of missiles, and footage broadcast on state TV this week claimed to show dozens of missiles at the entrance to an underground facility in southern Iran. Back in August, state TV footage also claimed to show Khordad surface-to-air missiles emerging out of a tunnel near the southern city of Bandar Abbas, external.A MAIAR analyst also identified new construction and excavations outside tunnel entrances near the city of Qom, close to the Fordo underground uranium enrichment complex, which has been bombed by both the US and Israel multiple times.Activity related to military assets would show that Tehran is bracing itself for further attacks by the US and Israel, said Mark Cancian, a military analyst with International Security Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS)."The purpose is to better defend itself against future attacks," he said. "It also indicates a priority on rebuilding military capability rather than rehabilitating the economy."Additional reporting by Barbara Metzler.

schema.headline: Major construction near Iran bases, satellite images suggest

title: Two dead after bus crashes in France, officials say
description: A young girl and an 18-year-old man have died after a bus crashed in eastern France, local authorities have said.The bus was travelling between Lyon a
body: A young girl and an 18-year-old man have died after a bus crashed in eastern France, local authorities have said.The bus was travelling between Lyon and Bourg-en-Bresse when it crashed at around 07:00 local time on Friday in the town of Lent.The bus was carrying 43 passengers, including 15 children, the Bourg-en-Bresse prosecutor's office said. Three people are in a critical condition and at least 13 others have sustained minor injuries.French President Emmanuel Macron said his thoughts were with the victims, the injured, and their families. In a post on X, he said the nation stood by their side and thanked the rescue teams involved.The town's mayor Yves Cristin told French media the bus "left the road and hit a tree in the ditch".The two people killed have been identified by authorities. However, there have been differing reports as to the age of the girl.The prosecutor's office said it was "opening an investigation into the incident, on charges of road homicide and aggravated road traffic injuries". The driver has been taken to hospital after sustaining injuries and has not yet been questioned by police. French Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot said initial tests indicated there were no traces of alcohol or drugs in his blood. Photos circulating in French media show a blue and white bus tilted in what appears to be a ditch on the roadside. Trees line the side of the road. The front of the bus appears to be heavily damaged.Local mayor Cristin told BFM TV: "I arrived minutes after the accident and people were in shock."The side of the bus was torn off, and clearly, the people who were on that side must have been seriously injured."Addressing weather conditions at the time of the crash, the mayor told Le Figaro "there was a bit of fog, the road was wet" but there were "no major difficulties". Speaking to the same paper, Fabrice Pannekoucke, head of the Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes region, said: "At this stage, there are no particular explanations or interpretations that can be given."Tabarot said the bus did not operate "exclusively on school routes" but that there were "many schoolchildren on board".

schema.headline: Two dead after bus crashes in France, officials say

title: Four midterms takeaways for 2028 White House race
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff and Republican Vice-President JD VanceByBernd Debusmann JrWhite House reporterBallot
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff and Republican Vice-President JD VanceByBernd Debusmann JrWhite House reporterBallots are still being counted in the US midterm elections but the political landscape is already pivoting to the 2028 White House race.Buoyed by major gains in Congress, Democrats will have momentum as they prepare for the contest to succeed President Donald Trump.But a good showing in the midterms does not guarantee a White House win two years later. Barack Obama was re-elected in 2012 despite huge Republican gains in 2010.No one has yet entered the presidential race but potential candidates will be preparing behind the scenes. Vice-President's JD Vance's reflection on where the midterms went wrong for Republicans has been interpreted as him paving the way for a 2028 run.The results of Tuesday's election and the historic size of Democratic gains could shape the White House race in several ways. Here are four takeaways.1. Big winners in the midterms now have momentumSeveral prominent potential presidential candidates were running in the 2026 midterms - and some emerged looking strong.Georgia Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff won by a sizeable margin in the politically competitive state that Trump won in 2024.While he has previously said he has no plans to run for president, his successful campaign, with several viral moments, helped boost his national profile.Another potential Democratic nominee, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, swept aside his Republican challenger. Shapiro has not committed to a 2028 run but analysts point to his broad appeal in swing-state Pennsylvania as a sign that he could be competitive on the national stage.Illinois Governor JB Pritzker also won after a campaign pundits in his state described as a "tune-up" for a presidential run.California Governor Gavin Newsom could not run for re-election in the midterms but he is invested in the outcome of a ballot initiative to tax the state's wealthy residents which he campaigned against.On the Republican side, there were two potential 2028 names running in Arkansas.Republican Senator Tom Cotton and Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders - a one-time Trump administration press secretary - were able to stay in office by a narrower margin than before, both earning just above half of the votes in the conservative state.2. JD Vance and Trump's allies under pressureExit polls suggest the swing against Republicans was partly due to anger felt by voters at the actions of the Trump administration.That could present a challenge to his potential successors who come from the ranks of the current leadership, including Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio."The one person who has been hurt badly by this election campaign is Vance," said Karen Beckwith, a professor of political science at Case Western Reserve University in Ohio.Vance has already sought to distance himself from defeat - and from a foreign policy adventure in Iran that was politically disastrous for his party."The reason we lost is the war," he wrote on X.Rubio has denied reports he is considering leaving his post ahead of a 2028 presidential run.Other possible Republican candidates may benefit from not being part of the administration. Some have been staking out a position on what went wrong and what next.In a lengthy post on X, Senator Ted Cruz, who was not running this year, said that too many Republican politicians seem like "they didn't care" about the economic issues faced by voters."It is dark right now, but it is always darkest before the dawn, and morning is coming," he wrote. "That is my fervent prayer, and that is my commitment to you."Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who abandoned his 2024 presidential run after being trounced by Trump early on, was similarly critical and pointed to Republican victories in Florida as a sign of what can be accomplished.3. Left and centre Democrats in fight for futureBoth the centrist and left wings of the Democratic Party have claimed victory from the results as each side sifts through possible 2028 contenders.Dozens are already making moves, Obama's former adviser Jim Messina has told the BBC.El-Sayed's win in Michigan was a breakthrough moment for left-wing Democrats because he triumphed in a swing state.His supporters now claim his win could supercharge left-wing candidates in the 2028 election."The old notions of electability are out the door, and bold economist populist outsiders proved they can win in battleground states," said Adam Green, the co-founder of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee.Green added that the "water is now warm" for candidates such as New York Democratic representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run in presidential primaries and "know that they can win."Moderate Democrats, however, claimed victories across the country, with the "Blue Dog Caucus" of moderate and conservative Democrats gaining at least 14 seats in Congress, nearly doubling its current size.This has led many within that wing of the party to conclude that centrist candidates that bill themselves as pragmatic and willing to work with conservatives could woo Republican voters.Given the success of Democratic candidates who focused on cost of living issues, an economy-first approach will likely be a focus again in two years.Amirah Siquierah, the director of federal affairs at the Working Families Party, said successful candidates in 2028 will combine economic populism with newer concerns such as data centres.4. Support of Hispanic voters must be earnedBoth parties must contend with a changing political map and a shifting coalition of support for 2028.Once "safe" Republican parts of the country can no longer be considered conservative strongholds. Texas is left with only one Republican at a statewide level, which means its 40 electoral college votes could be up for grabs in 2028.Christina Pascucci, a political commentator and one-time Senate candidate in California, said the midterms "challenge long-held political assumptions" and show that "neither party can afford to take its traditional strongholds for granted".That is true of both Democrats and Republicans who will need to win over swing voters, added Pascucci, now the CEO of Atlas Global, a global communications and advisory firm."Neither party owns these voters," she said.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Texas has a new Democratic governor, Gina HinojosaThe Trump coalition of working class and Latino voters faltered, reversing many of the gains he had made with those electorates in his successful 2024 campaign.Driena Sixto, a former spokesperson for Turning Point USA and a conservative political commentator, told the BBC that she believed that Republicans will have to change their messaging to Latino voters ahead of 2028 for any future candidate to be able to reverse the trend."Last time, the campaign message was one of safe communities and fighting back against trafficking," she said."After the president was sworn in, I think a lot of messaging from the White House did too much to highlight deportations. That was the divide."

schema.headline: Four midterms takeaways for 2028 White House race

title: Judge blocks construction of Donald Trump's massive arch
description: Judge blocks construction of Trump's massive arch after federal agency approvalFigure caption, Watch: Protesters demonstrate against Trump’s proposed
body: Judge blocks construction of Trump's massive arch after federal agency approvalFigure caption, Watch: Protesters demonstrate against Trump’s proposed archByNardine Saad and Isabella JewellReporting fromMemorial CircleUpdated 5 hours agoA federal judge has temporarily blocked construction of US President Donald Trump's "triumphal arch" in the nation's capital.US District Judge Tanya Chutkan ruled that there should be a 14-day pause before any work can start on the arch in Washington which the Trump administration had said could begin this week.  Earlier on Thursday the National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC) voted 8-4 to allow construction of the planned 250ft (72m) arch. Trump appointees on the board said the arch would be a fitting tribute to US history and to veterans but opponents have argued it would block the view of Arlington National Cemetery, the resting place of thousands of US soldiers and service people. The so-called Arc de Trump - a play on the name of the famous arch in Paris, the Arc de Triomphe - is one of the president's efforts to remake the capital city in his style and is meant to commemorate the country's 250th anniversary.The approval on Thursday evening came after nearly nine hours of public comment."The White House commends the National Capital Planning Commission's decision to fully approve President Trump's historic vision to build a much needed Triumphal Arch in Washington, DC," a White House spokesperson told the BBC in a statement.It is not yet clear  when construction of the arch could begin, as several lawsuits seek to block the project. The White House criticised the federal court that temporarily halted construction as an "activist district court.""We are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds and look forward to seeing the completion of this magnificent Arch," the spokesperson said.Image source, ReutersImage caption, An artist's rendering of Trump's proposed arch near Arlington CemeteryA rendering of the project's design from earlier this year includes a golden, winged Lady Liberty statue on the top of the arch, flanked by two gold eagles. The phrases "One Nation Under God" and "Liberty and Justice for All" are inscribed in gold on either side of the structure.A website that the White House shared on social media on Friday also shows a video rendering of the arch that shows the structure emblazoned with the words "Golden Age of America" along one side.It refers to the structure as "The Military Triumphal Arch".The proposed structure is sprinkled with appliques that are visually similar to the golden embellishments Trump has added to the Oval Office. The Trump administration has also said the arch would double as a complex to store military equipment - complete with the ability to deploy snipers and drones."There will be no facility like this anywhere in the World," Trump previously wrote on his Truth Social platform. He added that out of "the 59 top cities and Capitals", Washington is "the only one in the world that does not have a triumphal arch". He did not specify to which cities he was referring.Mark Paoletta, the chairman of the NCPC and one of the Trump appointees, said at Thursday's meeting that the president understood "it's important to our national identity to display who we are through grand monuments". How Trump is remaking the White House in his own imageHe and other commissioners said the structure fulfils a 100-year plan to build a monumental work on Columbia Island, just as Congress and various commissions intended. Paoletta added that the arch would honour the nation, its veterans and "provide the sacred ground of Arlington National Cemetery with the monumental gateway it deserves".Image caption, Anne Wright is among those who are opposed to the archOpponents have strongly disagreed. Anne Wright, who spent 29 years in the US military and also worked in the diplomatic service, told the BBC she would try to stop the construction."We'll tie ourselves to the bulldozer, we've got veterans in wheelchairs and we'll chain the wheelchairs to these things," she said.Wright referenced this week's midterm elections, in which Trump's Republican Party lost control of Congress, saying: "[Trump's] policy of war, of ego – they've been rejected."Fellow veteran John Pomeroy - who served in the Air Force for six years, including during the Vietnam War, and whose parents are buried at Arlington - said the arch "would lessen the solemn nature of a visit to the cemetery".He described Trump's suggestion that the arch could store military equipment as "silly" and a "half-baked idea", arguing it would be a target for terrorist attacks. Like Wright, Pomeroy said he would "impede construction workers as much as I can" if they came to the site to begin work.Democratic Congressman Jared Huffman argued in his statement to the commission that the arch would disrupt sightlines not just of Arlington but of the Lincoln Memorial, fracturing "a view meant to underscore the unity and sacrifice of the American people, and doing that with a structure we often associate with emperors or kings who built grand arches as tributes to themselves". "This is a tribute to Donald Trump," Huffman added.Lawsuits have been filed against the plans, raising concerns about the environment, traffic congestion and safety. There is also a disagreement over whether congressional approval is needed to build the arch. It is one of several construction projects Trump has proposed for the US capital. That includes at the White House, where he is facing legal challenges over the construction of a ballroom, which is estimated to cost $400m (£300m). His plans to renovate a 106-year-old golf course, which he has dubbed "trash island", is also being challenged in the courts.Rebecka Pieder contributed reporting.

schema.headline: Judge blocks construction of Donald Trump's massive arch

title: Tundu Lissu: Tanzania opposition leader found guilty of incitement but acquitted of treason
description: Tanzania's main opposition leader, Tundu Lissu, has been found guilty of inciting unrest and sentenced to four years in jail, in a case that has raise
body: Tanzania's main opposition leader, Tundu Lissu, has been found guilty of inciting unrest and sentenced to four years in jail, in a case that has raised concerns about political freedom in the East African country.A panel of three judges at the High Court in Dar es Salaam acquitted him of the more serious offence of treason, saying prosecutors had failed to prove a key element of that charge.But they said the 58-year-old, who has been detained since April last year, had encouraged his supporters to disrupt the disputed 2025 general election.Lissu, who leads the opposition Chadema party, has denied the charges, describing the prosecution as politically motivated.The court said his campaign slogan "No Reforms, No Election" was sufficient for him to be convicted of the charge of incitement."By uttering those words with the intention of disseminating them to the public, the accused incited the public to disrupt the 2025 elections," the court ruled.Lissu said he had only been charged with treason, not incitement."The offence of incitement is one that you, honourable judges, have manufactured. You have created an offence that did not exist, and you have done so on political directives," Lissu told the court. He added that he would like to apply for bail as this was possible for incitement, unlike treason.He has leave to appeal at the Court of Appeal - the country's highest court.But if the four-year sentence is upheld, it would rule him out of the next elections, due in 2030.Treason is among Tanzania's most serious offences and can carry the death penalty. Human rights group Amnesty International described his conviction as a "travesty of justice"."Tundu Lissu should never have been arrested, let alone prosecuted and convicted," said its regional director for East and Southern Africa, Tigere Chagutah:President Samia Suluhu Hassan won the October 2025 election with 98% of the vote - a result the opposition dismissed the result as a "mockery" of democracy as her two main challengers, including Lissu, were excluded.Her government has repeatedly denied targeting its opponents.During his time in remand custody at Dar es Salaam's Ukonga Prison, Lissu went on hunger strike twice for brief periods when he said he was not allowed access to his lawyers or relatives. He also complained that guards listened to what should have been private consultations his lawyers.These allegations have been denied by the prison authorities.His case has attracted international attention, with rights groups expressing concern about the treatment of opposition politicians and the shrinking space for political dissent in Tanzania.Last year's election was followed by widespread protests and a violent security crackdown that left at least 500 people dead, according to an official inquiry.Opposition groups have said the death toll was much higher and demanded an independent investigation.The government has defended its handling of the unrest and rejected accusations of widespread political repression.Samia, 66, has insisted the election was fair and transparent and blamed foreigners for the unrest, saying it was part of a plot to overthrow her. She has set up another commission to inquiry to identify those behind the violence.Lissu has long been one of Tanzania's most outspoken critics of the ruling Chama Cha Mapinduzi (CCM) party, which, along with its predecessor Tanu, has dominated the country's politics since independence.He first became an MP in 2010, representing a constituency near his birth place in Singida, 320km (200 miles) north-west of the capital, Dodoma.In September 2017, the Chadema politician narrowly survived an assassination attempt when gunmen sprayed his vehicle with bullets outside his home in Dodoma.He was shot multiple times and underwent extensive medical treatment abroad.The attack, whose perpetrators have never been brought to justice, forced him to spend years in exile.He returned to contest the 2020 presidential election against the late President John Magufuli, but lost in a vote that the opposition alleged was marred by widespread irregularities.Lissu subsequently returned to exile before coming back to Tanzania in 2023, following President Samia's decision to lift a ban on opposition political rallies.His return was initially seen as a sign of renewed political openness after years of restrictions under Magufuli, who died in office in 2021.But relations between the government and the opposition deteriorated as the country approached the 2025 election.Lissu became Chadema's national chairman in January 2025 and intensified his demands for electoral reforms.His conviction is likely to deepen concerns about the state of democracy in Tanzania.Last week, Amnesty accused the government of continuing its crackdown following the election and "weaponising counterterrorism laws to silence critics and instil fear".The authorities did not respond to a request for comment.Correction: An initial version of this story said Lissu had been convicted of inciting treason. We have corrected this to incitement.

schema.headline: Tundu Lissu: Tanzania opposition leader found guilty of incitement but acquitted of treason

title: Did a data centre revolt affect the US midterm election results?
description: Figure caption, BBC went to Arizona before the midterms to understand the data centre boom in the USByBen ChuPolicy and analysis correspondentA US mid
body: Figure caption, BBC went to Arizona before the midterms to understand the data centre boom in the USByBen ChuPolicy and analysis correspondentA US midterms voter poll has suggested data centres were a highly motivating issue for many Americans, leading some to argue public backlash against the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure construction boom might have helped shape the election outcome.BBC Verify has looked at its role in the campaign and examined the potential consequences for the AI industry.What did the voter poll suggest?The poll for AP and a consortium of news organisations found 56% of surveyed voters said data centres were a "crucial or major" factor in their vote, while 76% said they would oppose the construction of a new data centre in their community.The hostile sentiment was considerably stronger among those who said they voted Democrat at this election.This follows other recent Pew Research polling, external which suggested about half of Americans think data centres are "mostly bad" for the environment, home energy costs and quality of life, a big deterioration in favourability since January.The congressional voter poll results certainly suggest a remarkable degree of salience for a subject which likely would not have been on most Americans' radar five years ago.However, it is some way behind several key issues people considered a "crucial or major factor" in their vote, including government corruption (90%) and the cost of living (89%).Did the AI backlash affect Senate races?But other factors would also have been motivating voters in these states, as elsewhere.BBC Verify analysis of state-level voter polling for Senate elections suggests states which swung to the Democrats either followed the national trend over data centre concerns, or seemed less concerned.So we can't say how many votes or Senate seats were directly delivered by data centre opposition.But it's notable that three key states in the US AI build-out, Texas, Georgia and Ohio, all elected Democrats as senators and governors who called for tighter regulation on data centres in one form or another.These proposals include:temporary bans on constructionending tax breaksrequirements to fully cover their own energy and water infrastructure costsmandates to use unionised construction workersstricter environmental and transparency safeguardslocal rights to vetoWhat could the election results mean for the future of the AI boom?The US economy has been heavily supported in recent years by massive corporate investments in AI, external, including for data centre construction.Official data, external shows inflation-adjusted monthly spending on building data centres, excluding the IT hardware to go into them, in August 2026 was $5bn (£4.2bn) - five times higher than in 2023.Analysis by Columbia Business School, external suggests AI infrastructure investment in the US is currently larger as a share of the overall economy than spending on new railways was at the height of that boom in the 19th Century.Cori Crider, executive director of the Future of Tech Institute, a European think tank, told BBC Verify the industry should anticipate that new state leaders will put conditions on or "even stop runaway data centre build".Seema Shah, from global investment firm Principal Asset Management, said requirements for developers to pay for additional investment in the electricity grid, meet tougher standards over their usage of resources like water, or give up tax incentives could "raise development costs and slow new supply".Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The Stargate Oracle AI data centre spans roughly four million square feet in Abilene, TexasHowever, Heather West from the Eurasia Group consultancy said temporary bans on construction and new regulations might delay the data centre roll out, but would not stop it entirely.She said "projects already permitted or under construction will largely proceed", but delays would affect the "next wave" of building through "local fights, slower permitting, and pressure to make data centres pay for their own power".Analysts from the consultancy Oxford Economics have said there are also strong economic incentives for politicians to avoid policies that would severely disrupt data centre construction, pointing to tax revenue and construction jobs they bring.Deepak Surana of the Futurum Group, a technology research firm, said he expected there would ultimately be "a negotiation, not a moratorium" from Texas state leaders on data centres to ensure no negative impact on residents' energy and water bills.OpenAI, which has a data centre in Texas and under-construction projects in Ohio, pledged to ensure it fully paid for its own electricity on Thursday, external - one day after the midterm results.Additional reporting by Nicholas Barrett, Rob England and Christine JeavansGet in touchWhat are you hoping for from the Budget? What questions do you have?

schema.headline: Did a data centre revolt affect the US midterm election results?

title: New wave of bomb threats hit European airlines
description: A Ryanair flight scheduled to leave Lisbon for Rome on Friday was targeted with a threat, the airline said, while at least 11 flights were targeted in
body: A Ryanair flight scheduled to leave Lisbon for Rome on Friday was targeted with a threat, the airline said, while at least 11 flights were targeted in the Czech Republic and Bulgaria, according to AFP.France also reported at least four of its flights were targeted by threats, however they all landed safely. No explosives have been found on any planes as of Friday. As airlines were dealing with this latest wave of threats, several media outlets, including RTÉ, were evacuated after similar warnings were made against them. Staff at the Irish Independent newspaper and the Dublin offices of radio stations NewstalkFM and TodayFM, were also advised to leave their buildings and UK broadcaster Sky said it also received a security threat.In a statement, gardaí (Irish police) said they were "aware of a threat made against media organisations here and in Europe".While no link has been established between the threats against airlines and media outlets, the Irish government has warned it is a "likely coordinated campaign of disruption".In a statement, it said: "Hoax threats such as these cause fear, distress and disruption to people going about their daily lives and activities; they achieve no positive purpose whatsoever. It is not known yet who is responsible for these threats, whether it is individuals or a centralised or co-ordinated effort.Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin described the situation as "worrying" and added his government's first priority was the safety of the Irish public."Yesterday, there appeared to be coordinated efforts to disrupt air travel," he said.Martin told RTÉ it was not yet known if the threats had come from individuals or if it was a "coordinated attack" but said they were being taken seriously.Ireland is scheduled to host two high-profile European Union meetings in Dublin next week. Broadcaster Sky confirmed it had received a security threat, hours after RTÉ had evacuated its building.The broadcaster, which is owned by Comcast, said in a statement read by a presenter on its news channel that the broadcaster had "carried out a security assessment and reported the matter to the relevant authorities"."The safety and security of our colleagues is our primary concern, and we are working closely with authorities to ensure our people and operations remain secure."Friday's disruption comes after the Russian extremist group "Male State", named in this week's hoax bomb threats to Italian airports, denied any link to the false warnings.Replying to the BBC Russian Service, an account on Telegram - one of several linked to the so-called "Male State" and its founder Vladislav Pozdnyakov - mocked any suggestion the group was involved in emailing the threats."What Male State? Where have you seen it? It hasn't existed for many years," the message on the channel reads. "If tomorrow they sign a [threat] letter, say, from Putin, will you then try to reach our president to ask your stupid question?"

schema.headline: New wave of bomb threats hit European airlines

title: Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck
description: Tesla will wind down production of its Cybertruck vehicles at its Texas factory next year, Elon Musk says.He did not spell out whether it plans to sto
body: Tesla will wind down production of its Cybertruck vehicles at its Texas factory next year, Elon Musk says.He did not spell out whether it plans to stop making them entirely or shift production elsewhere, but did say the decision was to "make room" for building more of its self-driving Cybercab cars.But the project's lead engineer, Wes Morrill, appeared to suggest the vehicle was being discontinued, writing on X: "Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab."With its distinctive angular looks, the Cybertruck attracted diehard fans, but was beset by delays before being launched in 2023 and has had disappointing sales numbers since.Tesla fans have been mourning the news online, with one person calling it "the best vehicle Tesla has ever made, external" as he lamented it being "discontinued next year".Musk responded to the user, external with the word "true", adding: "But the Cybertruck fleet will be around for a long time."The vehicle has always been a passion project for Musk. He said it was "way more awesome than people realise, external" in March, and called it the "best product Tesla has ever made to date, external" in April.But there have always been big questions about whether consumers shared that view and whether the Cybertruck could cut through and earn a spot in the US' lucrative truck market.It was not helped by inauspicious introduction to the public in 2019 when Musk attempted to show off the Cybertruck's apparently unbreakable glass, only for it to shatter during a live demonstration.

schema.headline: Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck

title: Somalia's Supreme court rejects President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud's term extension
description: Somalia's Supreme Court has ruled that President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud unlawfully extended his term, escalating a political crisis and a standoff betw
body: Somalia's Supreme Court has ruled that President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud unlawfully extended his term, escalating a political crisis and a standoff between the presidency and judiciary.Thursday's ruling came a day after Mohamud dismissed Chief Justice Bashe Yusuf Ahmed - a move which the court said the president lacked the authority to take.The court also ordered political leaders to agree on an electoral plan within 30 days and hold elections within 90 days, potentially disrupting government plans for nationwide polls next year.Mohamud's four-year mandate expired in May, but his administration extended it by a year through law changes approved by parliament in March.Opposition groups accuse him of using the constitutional changes to prolong his rule. But the president insists the reforms are necessary to move Somalia towards fully democratic elections, replacing the clan-based system in which elders pick their representatives which has been used since 2012.Somalia last held nationwide direct elections in 1969 and has been wracked by civil war for more than 30 years, with Islamist militant group al-Shabab controlling many rural areas.On Thursday, the Supreme Court ruled that the constitutional changes could not be applied retrospectively to the president's current term.In a separate decision, the court declared the chief justice's dismissal "null and void", accusing the presidency of interfering with judicial independence.The president appointed Ibrahim Idle Suleiman, who previously held the position, to replace Ahmed.The presidency said the dismissal followed complaints about the administration of justice and was intended to achieve a just and transparent judiciary. But the court rejected that explanation, insisting that the chief justice could only be removed through established constitutional procedures.Former President Sharif Sheikh Ahmed welcomed the court ruling, saying "the country is facing a grave political crisis", calling on Mohamud to embrace a consensus-based approach. The confrontation escalated on Thursday when former Prime Minister Hassan Ali Khaire accused the president of deploying security forces to the Supreme Court and attempting to arrest its chief justice.Khaire accused the president of launching an "assault on the Supreme Court", according to the AFP news agency."Somalia stands at a dangerous juncture. The dismantling of our judiciary is a direct threat to the rule of law," he said.AFP said it could not independently verify the reported security deployment, although photographs circulating in Somali media appeared to show armed personnel inside the court compound.The rulings have thrown Somalia's electoral timetable into uncertainty.The electoral commission has scheduled parliamentary elections for 15 April 2027 and a presidential vote a month later, but opposition groups and the regional administrations of Puntland and Jubaland reject the timetable.Mohamud has called for national talks from 14 to 18 November to resolve the deadlock, but opposition leaders have questioned his legitimacy to convene the discussions.The political turmoil comes as Somalia continues to battle al-Shabab, which controls large parts of the countryside despite years of military operations.Uganda, the largest contributor of troops to the African Union mission fighting the militants, announced this week that it planned to withdraw its forces by the end of the year, adding to concerns about Somalia's security.

schema.headline: Somalia's Supreme court rejects President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud's term extension

title: Dozens of Democrats eyeing 2028 presidential run, says former Obama aide
description: More than two dozen Democrats are eyeing runs for the White House in 2028, following their party's success in the US midterm elections this week, acco
body: More than two dozen Democrats are eyeing runs for the White House in 2028, following their party's success in the US midterm elections this week, according to the man behind Barack Obama's successful re-election bid.Jim Messina, who led Obama's 2012 campaign, said that since Democrats saw major victories in congressional races as well as state elections, he's spoken to "over two dozen campaigns" that are actively considering running in 2028 and have begun the financing process and hiring staff."I think you're going to start having Democrats announce exploratory committees next week or the next couple of weeks, probably after Thanksgiving", Messina told the BBC's Americast podcast.He said he already knows someone relocating to work on a governor's presidential campaign.He also predicted that the number could shrink as candidates faced pressure to raise large sums needed for the primary contests that will decide the party's nominee.Messina gave some insight into the conversations he's had, saying:  "When I sit down with candidates or their campaigns, I say to them, 'Tell me your economic vision for the future of this country. What are you going to do on AI?'"Then there's another factor: the outgoing president, Donald Trump, who will still be in office during the campaign season."And so, do the Democrats take the bait and talk about Donald Trump every day, or do you stay focused on your message?" he said."It's going be the most interesting presidential [election] since 2008."Messina, who went on to become Obama's deputy chief of staff at the White House, said the party's success in the US midterm elections was down to their ability to stay focused on the economy and the effect of Donald Trump's tariffs, which were "devastating to rural voters"."When you're a farmer and you're paying $7 for a gallon of diesel to put in your tractor, the economics just don't work, and at the same time you're paying more for everything," he said.PODCAST: Hear more from Jim Messina on AmericastStaying on message about the economy helped them flip seats in traditionally strong Republican states like Iowa, Kansas, and Texas, he said."The common criticism of Democrats is that we can't stick to one message. And for the first time in a very long time, Democrats stuck to the economy. They didn't take the bait on the social wars," he said. Messina cautioned Democrats that success in this year's midterm elections was not a ringing endorsement of the party and that "the MVP of the election for the Democrats was Donald Trump".The hard part will now be bringing the party's progressive and centrist wings together in Congress, he said.

schema.headline: Dozens of Democrats eyeing 2028 presidential run, says former Obama aide

title: Russian extremist group denies sending hoax bomb threats
description: The "Male State", an extremist misogynistic group named in this week's hoax bomb threats to Italian airports, has denied any link to the false warning
body: The "Male State", an extremist misogynistic group named in this week's hoax bomb threats to Italian airports, has denied any link to the false warnings causing flight disruption across Europe.The comments to the BBC came as reports of more bomb scares to airlines began appearing, including on a Ryanair flight from Rome to Lisbon and a Wizz Air flight from Prague to Rome which was diverted to Venice.Bomb threats were also reported to a number of high-profile Irish media organisations on Friday, prompting evacuations and a statement from the Irish government suggesting a "co-ordinated campaign of disruption".Replying to the BBC Russian Service, an account on Telegram - one of several linked to the so-called "Male State" and its founder Vladislav Pozdnyakov - mocked any suggestion the group was involved in emailing the threats."What Male State? Where have you seen it? It hasn't existed for many years," the message on the channel reads. "If tomorrow they sign a [threat] letter, say, from Putin, will you then try to reach our president to ask your stupid question?"The group was banned in Russia in 2021 and Pozdnyakov is now thought to live abroad. It has since renamed itself in some places as "Male Legion".The initial hoax email, seen by the BBC, was sent on Thursday at 07:21 with the subject title: warning of a threat.It was addressed to several offices and individuals at Aeroporti di Roma (ADR), the airport managing company in Rome, as well as accounts at the city's Fiumicino airport itself. The originating email address seems to be linked to the state health services in Bogota, Colombia.It's not clear whether other countries' airports or airlines received the same or similar threat. At least one warning made on Friday appears to have come by phone, not email.Written in word perfect Italian, the bizarre text sent to Rome on Thursday claimed that "fighters" of the "Male State" had planted explosives on two incoming flights in an attack on Italy's "feminist regime" that would be "remembered forever".One flight was diverted as a result - ordered to land in France – another was escorted into Rome by Italian air force jets, scrambled for the second time this week. No explosives were found on either plane, or any other that reported receiving bomb threats.Asked why this particular email was taken so seriously, a source at ADR in Rome told the BBC that such warnings were extremely unusual. They didn't remember anything similar in recent years.Despite the Russian group's denial, Italy's La Stampa newspaper appears in no doubt that "Male State" was behind the threats, asking in an article whether it is acting as "the regime's armed wing"."Attacking, and being able to deny the attacks...is part of the Russian game plan," the paper writes, external.One Telegram channel linked to Pozdnyakov is mainly filled with virulently pro-Russian messaging about the war on Ukraine and other posts highlighting problems and tensions in Europe, including recent youth protests.The online investigation team at Bellingcat, who studied the group back in 2022, called it then a "vocal and vile online booster" of the Russian invasion, with a clear extremist far-right ideology.As the Europe-wide hunt continues for who is behind the spate of hoax mails, and whether they are being co-ordinated - or could be the work of copycats - Italy's defence minister has warned of a "strategy to increase chaos".Guido Crosetto noted that he had been talking of the "hybrid threat" to Europe for some years."It seems to me that, day after day, from incidents involving refrigerators to the blood supply in France and now these false alarms, there are those who have an interest in fuelling tensions," the minister said on Thursday, referring to a spate of recent cyber attacks that boosted supermarket fridge temperatures, destroying mountains of produce."Our interest is to do the opposite and ensure the country's security," Crosetto said.Additional reporting by Davide Ghiglione

schema.headline: Russian extremist group denies sending hoax bomb threats
